learn.hook: You can take a packet of biscuits home, but you cannot take home a haircut or a train ride. Services are different from goods in five important ways.
points: Services are intangible, essential activities that satisfy needs. Goods are tangible products that can be seen, touched and stored.

Five Is of services: Intangibility (cannot be touched; the experience matters); Inconsistency (quality varies each time and with each customer); Inseparability (production and consumption happen together); Inventory (less) (services cannot be stored for later); Involvement (the customer takes part in the delivery).

Goods vs services: tangible vs intangible; goods are fairly homogeneous, services are heterogeneous; goods can be stored, services cannot; ownership of goods passes to the buyer, but services give only an experience; goods can be returned, services cannot.

Business services are used by firms to conduct activities: banking, insurance, transportation, warehousing and communication. Social services are provided voluntarily for social goals, e.g. NGOs offering health care or education. Personal services are experienced differently by each customer, e.g. tourism, recreation, restaurants.

example.q: An empty seat on a flight that took off this morning cannot be sold tomorrow. Which feature of services does this show?
steps: The seat-service existed only for that flight's time.
It could not be stored and sold later.
This is the feature of no inventory.

Answer: business services

options: A is false, but R is true

learn.hook: Your monthly pocket money, your father's home loan and the cheque your aunt sends on your birthday all pass through one institution: the bank.
points: A bank accepts deposits of money from the public for the purpose of lending or investment, repayable on demand or otherwise, and withdrawable by cheque, draft or order (as per the Banking Regulation Act, 1949).

Types of banks: commercial banks (public sector, where the government holds the majority, and private sector); cooperative banks (under state cooperative laws, giving cheap credit to members); specialised banks (foreign exchange banks, industrial banks, development banks, export-import banks); and the central bank (the Reserve Bank of India, which supervises and regulates banks and controls money supply).

Functions of commercial banks: accepting deposits; lending of funds (loans, overdraft, cash credit, discounting of bills); cheque facility (bearer and crossed cheques); remittance of funds (bank drafts, pay orders, electronic transfers); allied services (bill payments, lockers, buying and selling shares, underwriting).
Banks earn mainly from the difference between the interest they charge on loans and the interest they pay on deposits.

example.q: A bank pays 6% interest per year on deposits of ₹10,00,000 and lends the whole amount at 10% per year. What is its gross interest margin for the year?
steps: Interest earned = 10% of 10,00,000 = ₹1,00,000.
Interest paid = 6% of 10,00,000 = ₹60,000.

learn.hook: A college student, a supermarket owner and a retired teacher all need very different bank accounts. Picking the wrong one means losing either interest or convenience.
points: Savings account: encourages savings by individuals; earns interest; limits on withdrawals may apply. Current account: for businessmen, with no limit on the number of transactions; usually no interest; overdraft facility possible.

Recurring deposit (RD): a fixed amount deposited every month for a fixed period; earns higher interest than savings. Fixed deposit (FD): a lump sum deposited for a fixed period; earns higher interest; penalty on premature withdrawal.

Multiple option deposit account: a savings account in which the amount above a set limit is automatically transferred into a fixed deposit, and FDs are broken automatically when the savings balance is insufficient, so the customer gets both liquidity and higher interest.

Remittance: a bank draft is an order by a bank to its branch (or another bank) to pay a specified sum, used to send money to another place; a pay order (banker's cheque) is used for payment within the same city.

Overdraft: a current-account holder may withdraw more than his balance up to a sanctioned limit; interest is charged only on the amount overdrawn. Cash credit: the bank sanctions a cash loan limit against security of current assets (such as stock); interest is charged on the amount actually used.

example.q: Kiran has an overdraft limit of ₹1,00,000 on her current account with ₹20,000 balance. She issues a cheque of ₹70,000. How much is overdrawn, and on what amount is interest charged?
steps: Balance available = ₹20,000.
₹50,000 is within the ₹1,00,000 limit.
Interest is charged only on the overdrawn ₹50,000.

learn.hook: Your parents may remember standing in long bank queues to send money. Today it takes seconds on a phone. That revolution is e-banking.
points: E-banking (electronic banking) means using the internet, mobile phones and electronic networks to carry out banking transactions. It is also called internet or online banking.

Services: Electronic Fund Transfer (EFT); National Electronic Funds Transfer (NEFT), which settles transfers in batches; Real Time Gross Settlement (RTGS), which settles each transaction individually and instantly, generally for large amounts; Automated Teller Machines (ATMs); debit cards (money is deducted from the account at once); credit cards (spending on credit up to a limit, paid later); internet and mobile banking.

Benefits to customers: banking 24 hours a day, 365 days a year; transactions from anywhere (office, home, while travelling); a record of every transaction, giving financial discipline; greater customer satisfaction.
Benefits to banks: competitive advantage; unlimited network, not limited by the number of branches; less load on branches because of centralised databases.

example.q: A company must pay a large amount to a supplier immediately and wants each payment settled individually in real time. Which service should it use?
steps: Real time = settled at once, not in batches.
Gross settlement = each transaction settled individually.
Large-value urgent transfers suit RTGS.

learn.reallife: UPI and net banking let a kirana owner in a small town pay a wholesaler in Mumbai at midnight, something impossible when branches were the only option.

learn.hook: A vegetable seller in your colony now has a QR code taped to her cart. India's digital payment story has reached every street corner.
points: Digital payments are payments made through digital or online modes, with no physical exchange of cash.

Banking cards (debit, credit and prepaid cards); USSD (Unstructured Supplementary Service Data), using *99# for banking on basic phones without internet; AEPS (Aadhaar Enabled Payment System), for transactions using Aadhaar authentication at micro ATMs or with business correspondents.

UPI (Unified Payments Interface): links multiple bank accounts into one mobile app for instant transfers using a virtual payment address; developed by the National Payments Corporation of India (NPCI).
Mobile wallets: store money digitally on a phone for quick payments; bank prepaid cards: loaded in advance with a fixed amount.

Point of Sale (PoS) terminals: card-swiping or tap machines at shops; internet banking and mobile banking; micro ATMs: small devices used by business correspondents to provide basic banking in remote areas.

example.q: A farmer in a village has a basic phone without internet and wants to check his balance and transfer money. Which digital mode suits him?
steps: No internet rules out UPI apps and internet banking.
USSD works on basic phones by dialling *99#.

learn.reallife: UPI, developed by NPCI, is used everywhere from chai stalls to big malls; India now records billions of UPI transactions every month.

learn.hook: A thousand shopkeepers each pay a small amount; when fire hits one shop, the pool pays for the damage. That simple idea of pooling risk is insurance.
points: Insurance is a contract in which one party (the insurer) agrees, in return for a consideration (the premium), to compensate the other party (the insured) for loss caused by specified risks. The document is the policy.
It works on pooling of risk: many people facing a similar risk contribute premiums to a common fund, from which the few who suffer loss are paid.

Functions: providing certainty (of payment against uncertain loss); protection (against loss from the event, though not against the event itself); risk sharing (loss is shared by all who pay premiums); assisting in capital formation (premiums collected are invested in productive activities).
Insurance does not prevent fire or accidents; it only reduces their financial impact.

example.q: 2,000 shop owners each pay a premium of ₹1,500 into an insurance pool. In a year, fire damage to some shops totals ₹25,00,000. Is the pool enough to pay the losses?
steps: 30,00,000 > 25,00,000, so the pool can pay all claims.
example.answer: Yes. The pool of ₹30,00,000 covers losses of ₹25,00,000.

learn.reallife: LIC invests a large share of the premiums it collects in government securities and infrastructure: insurance helping capital formation.

learn.hook: A shopkeeper insures his goods worth ₹5 lakh with two companies and expects ₹10 lakh after a fire. Seven principles of insurance explain why he won't get it.
points: Utmost good faith (uberrimae fidei): both parties must disclose all material facts honestly. Insurable interest: the insured must have a financial interest in the subject matter, i.e. he suffers a loss if it is damaged.
Indemnity: the insurer compensates only the actual loss, up to the sum insured; the insured cannot profit from insurance. It applies to fire and marine insurance, not to life insurance.
Proximate cause (causa proxima): when loss results from two or more causes, the nearest (most direct) cause decides whether the loss is covered.
Subrogation: after paying the claim, the insurer takes over the insured's rights over the damaged property (e.g. salvage) and against third parties.

Contribution: if the same property is insured with more than one insurer, they share the loss in proportion to the sums insured; the insured cannot recover more than the actual loss. Mitigation: the insured must take reasonable steps to minimise loss, like an uninsured person would.

example.q: Goods worth ₹6,00,000 are insured with Insurer A for ₹4,00,000 and Insurer B for ₹2,00,000. Fire causes a loss of ₹3,00,000. How much does each insurer pay?
steps: By contribution, loss is shared in that ratio.
By indemnity, the insured gets exactly ₹3,00,000, no more.

learn.hook: Life insurance is often called 'life assurance' because death is certain; only its timing is not.
points: Life insurance: a contract in which the insurer, in return for premium, agrees to pay a sum on the death of the insured or on the expiry of a fixed period, whichever is earlier, depending on the policy. It is a contract of protection and investment, not of indemnity.
Elements: it is a valid contract; utmost good faith; insurable interest at the time of taking the policy; it is not a contract of indemnity; the amount is paid on death or maturity.

Policies: whole life (sum paid only on death of the insured, to beneficiaries); endowment (sum paid at maturity, or on earlier death); joint life (two or more lives insured, usually spouses or partners; sum paid on the first death to the survivor(s)); annuity (sum paid in instalments after the insured reaches a certain age); children's endowment (for children's education or marriage, paid when the child reaches a certain age).

Health insurance covers medical and hospital expenses due to illness or injury. With rising medical costs, it protects families from large unexpected bills; many policies offer cashless treatment at network hospitals.

example.q: Anil, 35, wants a policy that pays him a lump sum at 55 to fund his retirement, but pays his family if he dies before 55. Which policy suits him?
steps: Payment at maturity (age 55) or on earlier death = endowment policy.

learn.reallife: Government schemes such as Ayushman Bharat-PMJAY provide health cover to crores of families, showing how important health insurance is in India.

topics.title: Fire and marine insurance; comparing the three

learn.hook: A ship carrying Indian basmati to the Gulf faces storms and pirates; the godown storing it faces fire. Different risks need different insurance.
points: Fire insurance: the insurer agrees, for a premium, to compensate the insured for loss or damage to property from fire during a specified period, up to the sum insured. Elements: insurable interest both at the time of contract and at the time of loss; utmost good faith; indemnity; the loss must be caused by actual fire (or flame); the fire must be accidental, not intentional; proximate cause.

Marine insurance covers risks of sea voyages. Hull insurance covers the ship (vessel); cargo insurance covers the goods on board; freight insurance covers the freight the shipping company would lose if the goods are lost and do not reach the destination.
Insurable interest: life – at the time of the contract; fire – both at the contract and at the time of loss; marine – at the time of loss.

Indemnity: not applicable to life; applicable to fire and marine. Duration: life is long-term; fire is usually for one year; marine is for a voyage or a period. Surrender value: only life insurance policies have a surrender value.

example.q: A shipping company fears that if a vessel sinks, it will not be paid its freight charges. Which marine insurance should it buy?
steps: The risk is the loss of freight income, not of the ship or goods.
That is covered by freight insurance.

learn.hook: India Post has one of the largest postal networks in the world, reaching villages where no bank branch exists. It does far more than deliver letters.
points: Financial facilities: savings schemes such as the Public Provident Fund (PPF), Kisan Vikas Patra, National Savings Certificate, recurring deposit and monthly income scheme; money orders to transfer money.

Mail facilities: parcel (transmission of articles from one place to another); registered post (safe delivery, with proof of posting and delivery); insured post (for valuable articles; the post office compensates loss or damage in transit up to the insured value).

Allied facilities: greetings post (greeting cards), media post (brands can advertise on postcards, letters and post boxes), direct post (direct advertising material delivered to targeted homes), international money transfer, passport facilities, speed post (fast, time-bound delivery), e-bill post (collecting bill payments), and courier services.
Project idea: visit a nearby post office or bank, note the services offered and how customers use them, and present your findings.
Note: this course follows the CBSE 2026-27 syllabus, so the transport, warehousing and telecom parts of the printed book are not covered.
